title: North Washington CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Around North Washington the median well depth is 30 ft with a 33 gpm median yield. Here’s what that means for drilling cost and water reliability.
h1: Water wells around North Washington, Colorado
intro_html:
North Washington sits on the Denver Basin, but the wells right around here are surprisingly shallow compared to most of the metro fringe. With thousands of permits on file in a 5‑mile radius, we’ve got a good picture of how deep wells run, how much water they make, and what they typically cost.

If you’re looking at land near Twin Lakes, Welby, Sherrelwood, Berkley, Derby or Federal Heights, the same numbers generally apply. Below is what I’d want a buyer to know before budgeting for a new well or judging an existing one.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in North Washington
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of North Washington, the median well depth on record is only 30 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 45 feet. About 91% of wells are under 100 feet, and only 3% fall in each of the 100–300, 300–600, and 600+ foot brackets. The deepest well on record is 1,751 feet, but that’s an outlier, not what you plan around.

For bidding, most drillers will assume a shallow domestic well, but they also know Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock can vary. I’d plan your budget around a shallow to moderate hole, while keeping in mind that a few locations do end up much deeper if they chase a different part of the aquifer system.

sections.heading: Water table and long‑term trend here
sections.html:
Static water levels reported around North Washington are very shallow. The median depth to water is 11 feet, and the middle half runs from 7 to 23 feet. That’s about as easy as it gets from a pumping standpoint, and it also explains why so many wells don’t need much depth.

The long‑term numbers don’t show a dropping table. Median static level was 37 feet in the 1960s, then 11 feet in the 2010s, and 9 feet in the 2020s. That shift toward shallower levels suggests the alluvial and Denver Basin interface here has stayed strong, likely helped by nearby surface‑water influences and return flows in this part of Adams County.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you actually get
sections.html:
Productivity around North Washington is solid. Of the wells that report a pump test, the median yield is 33.0 gpm, with the middle half between 13.0 and 101.0 gpm. About 72% of reported wells make 15+ gpm, 23% fall in the 5–15 gpm range, and 4% are between 1–5 gpm. None of the reported wells are under 1 gpm.

For a household well, anything above about 5 gpm is usually workable, and this area is mostly well above that. High‑yield numbers in the double and even triple digits also make small irrigation setups more realistic on the right permit, though only about 3% of permits here are actually for irrigation use.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how active it is
sections.html:
There’s a long history of well work around North Washington. The records show 331 permits from the 1950s and 298 from the 1960s, then 187 in the 1970s. Activity picked up in the 1980s with 548 permits and really accelerated in the 1990s with 2,011 and the 2000s with 1,733.

The 2010s were even busier at 2,868 permits, and there are already 1,053 in the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. Authorized (Pe, Pg) has 3,846 wells in the records, Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.) 236, and Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.) 111. Every well is listed in a Denver Basin aquifer, with a lot of permits simply calling it an unnamed or fractured‑bedrock aquifer, plus alluvial units like Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium.

sections.heading: Typical cost to drill a new well here
sections.html:
The ground around North Washington is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and local drill pricing usually runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 30 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $1,500–$2,100. That matches what drillers see for a straightforward short well.

Once you add pump, pressure tank, pitless adapter, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well here typically comes in roughly between $7,500 and $14,100. Deeper holes toward the upper end of the local range, or more complex trenching and power runs, push you toward the top of that band. Even so, compared to deeper Denver Basin areas, North Washington is on the less expensive side strictly on a per‑well basis.

sections.heading: Environmental and low‑yield risks to think through
sections.html:
From a quantity standpoint, this area is favorable: none of the reported wells come in under 1 gpm, and only 4% are between 1–5 gpm. Still, a small share of wells fall low enough that you should read each permit’s pump‑test data before you buy. Domestic/household use makes up about 12% of permits, irrigation about 3%, and a large share, 67%, are monitoring wells, which tells you regulators watch this area closely.

Within about 10 miles there are 689 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 189 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, plus 1 historic mine feature. That doesn’t mean your specific well is bad, but it does mean water‑quality testing for PFAS and common contaminants is not optional here.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in North Washington
sections.html:
There are 11,217 wells in the state records within about 5 miles of North Washington, and 6,228 of those report a depth. That density of data is useful when you’re evaluating a parcel. Look up the closest half‑dozen domestic wells and pay attention to their depths, static water levels, and yields, not just the median numbers.

If the lot already has a well, confirm its permit use (domestic, irrigation, monitoring) and check the reported static level against the area median of 11 feet. For new construction, coordinate well, septic, and house placement early to avoid setbacks and to keep your well uphill from future leach fields. In this part of Adams County, tying your building plans to a solid understanding of the Denver Basin and local alluvium saves expensive redesigns later.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around North Washington, Colorado?
faq.a: Around North Washington the median well depth is 30 feet, with the middle half of wells between 20 and 45 feet. About 91% of wells are under 100 feet, and only a small share reach 100–300, 300–600, or 600+ feet. The deepest well on record hits 1,751 feet, but that is not typical for most domestic or small‑parcel wells in this area.

faq.q: How much water do North Washington wells usually produce?
faq.a: Reported wells around North Washington have a median pump yield of 33.0 gpm, with the middle half ranging from 13.0 to 101.0 gpm. About 72% of wells make 15+ gpm, 23% fall in the 5–15 gpm range, and 4% are between 1–5 gpm. None of the reported wells produce under 1 gpm, so outright “trickle” wells are rare in the local dataset.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well near North Washington, CO?
faq.a: In Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock around North Washington, drilling typically runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 30 feet, that’s roughly $1,500–$2,100 for the hole itself. A complete domestic setup with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals about $7,500–$14,100, depending on depth, power distance, and specific site conditions.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near North Washington?
faq.a: The available static water level data do not show a dropping water table. Median depth to water was 37 feet in the 1960s, then 11 feet in the 2010s, and 9 feet in the 2020s. The overall median static level across records is 11 feet, with the middle half of readings between 7 and 23 feet, indicating relatively shallow groundwater in this area over time.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in North Washington, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Within about 10 miles there are 689 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 189 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, plus 1 historic mine feature. Those numbers mean you should always test your well, especially for PFAS and routine potability parameters. Many homes use wells safely here, but it’s the lab results that matter for your parcel.
